title: Elasticity

notes.heading: 1. Stress, Strain, Hooke's Law & Material Moduli (Y, K, η)
notes.proseLatex: Within the proportional limit, restoring stress $\sigma = F/A$ ($\text{N/m}^2$ or $\text{Pa}$) is proportional to dimensionless strain $\varepsilon$. Longitudinal stretch gives Young's modulus $Y = \frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$ (equivalent spring stiffness $k_{\text{wire}} = \frac{YA}{L}$), hydrostatic pressure gives Bulk modulus $K = -\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$ (compressibility $\beta = 1/K$), and tangential shear gives rigidity modulus $\eta = \frac{F_t/A}{\theta}$. Steel has a higher Young's modulus than rubber, making steel MORE elastic in physics!

keyFormulas.label: Young's, Bulk & Shear Moduli + Wire Stiffness
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Treat stretched rods as springs of stiffness YA/L and compare elastic moduli.

examples.problemLatex: Two wires of the SAME material have length ratio $L_1:L_2 = 1:2$ and radius ratio $r_1:r_2 = 2:1$. Under equal tension $F$, find $\Delta L_1 : \Delta L_2$.
stepsLatex: Same material means $Y_1 = Y_2$; from $\Delta L = \frac{FL}{\pi r^2 Y}$, $\Delta L \propto \frac{L}{r^2}$.

notes.heading: 2. Poisson's Ratio & Inter-Modulus Relations
notes.proseLatex:
Stretching a wire longitudinally causes lateral contraction, defining Poisson's ratio $
u = - rac{\Delta r/r}{\Delta L/L}$ with thermodynamic bounds $-1 \le 
u \le 0.5$ ($0 < 
u < 0.5$ for engineering metals; $
u = 0.5$ corresponds to constant volume $ rac{\Delta V}{V} = (1 - 2
u) rac{\Delta L}{L} = 0$). Isotropic elastic constants obey $Y = 3K(1 - 2
u) = 2\eta(1 + 
u)$.

keyFormulas.label: Poisson's Ratio & Isotropic Modulus Identities
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Link Y, K, eta and Poisson's ratio nu, and test constant-volume stretching.

notes.heading: 3. Elastic Potential Energy & Thermal Clamped Stress
notes.proseLatex: Slowly stretching or hanging a load (at equilibrium) stores elastic energy $U = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$ (when a dead weight $mg$ drops by $\Delta L$, gravity does work $mg\Delta L$, storing $\frac{1}{2}mg\Delta L$ elastically and dissipating the other $\frac{1}{2}mg\Delta L$ as heat!). Elastic energy density per unit volume is $u = \frac{U}{AL} = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma^2}{2Y} = \frac{1}{2}Y\varepsilon^2$. A rod clamped rigidly between walls and heated by $\Delta T$ develops compressive thermal stress $\sigma_{\text{th}} = Y\alpha\Delta T$ (independent of length $L$!).

keyFormulas.label: Elastic Energy Density & Thermal Stress
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute stored energy per unit volume and clamped thermal force.

examples.problemLatex: A steel rod ($Y = 2\times 10^{11}\text{ Pa},\; \alpha = 1.2\times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}$) of area $A = 5\text{ cm}^2$ is rigidly clamped and heated by $50\text{ K}$. Find the compressive force on the supports.

wbjeebTraps: Young's modulus $Y$ is an intrinsic MATERIAL property: doubling wire length or halving radius does NOT change $Y$!
Elastic energy stored is $\frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$, NOT $F\Delta L$ — don't drop the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor.
Clamped thermal force $F = YA\alpha\Delta T$ is completely INDEPENDENT of the rod's original length $L$.
